extracted: The authors note a decline over time in the proportion of participants reporting a non-fatal overdose, the most substantial during 2001, and write that it is consistent with other reports of a reduction in heroin-related overdoses during this period (Wood et al., 2006, as cited) and suggests that global reductions in heroin supply may have played a role; it may also be related to the protective effect of methadone treatment and the significant expansion of methadone treatment availability in British Columbia from 1995 to 2004 (Anderson and Warren, 2004, as cited). They also note that a supervised injection facility had recently opened in Vancouver and that its impact on overdose had not yet been evaluated. Limitations: VIDUS is not a random sample, so the findings may not generalize to other populations of people who inject drugs; overdoses were self-defined by participants asked whether they had had an overdose in the past 6 months, an approach the authors say may introduce an element of subjectivity but offers advantages where polysubstance use is the norm, adding that the definitions used in previous studies also introduce limitations related to recall bias and do not provide a hard diagnosis of overdose; the exact temporal relationship between the outcome and the explanatory variables could not be ascertained, so the study does not allow a thorough investigation of causal relationships; and although it has been suggested that changing drug purity may play a role in predicting overdose (Darke et al., 1999, as cited), the authors were unable to consider it. Editors' notes: the study recorded no measure of heroin supply, availability, price or purity, so its explanation of the decline rests on the papers it cites. The letter (anchor 9) says these authors clearly point to reduced heroin supply as the reason; the paper says reduced supply may have played a role and adds methadone expansion as a possible reason. The paper it cites for the reduction in heroin-related overdoses (Wood et al., 2006, volume 101, pages 689–95, on Canadian heroin supply) is the letter's reference 3, dated 2004 there, and the study's own reference 44 (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 1434, 1437); read since from its PDF (anchors 19 to 22), it reports fewer overdose deaths across British Columbia and fewer naloxone-requiring ambulance responses in the Downtown Eastside in 2001–03 than in 1998–2000, and measured no heroin purity.

extracted: A paper by five authors, three of them authors of the study (Wood, Montaner and Kerr), on markers of heroin use and harm in western Canada before and after the Australian heroin shortage, which it dates from about January 2001. Its stated primary hypothesis was that the markers would stay stable or rise, because western Canada receives heroin from similar source countries and, citing one paper, had not changed its supply-reduction funding or activities since the mid-1990s. It compared yearly averages, with no statistical test and no comparison series, of overdose deaths in the whole province of British Columbia from the provincial vital statistics registry, 1998–2000 against 2001–03 (the drugs responsible were not available, and some deaths would probably not involve heroin); ambulance responses that required naloxone in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside, fiscal years 1997–98 to 2000–01 against 2001–02 to 2002–03; and the weight of heroin destined for Canada that was seized, 1998–2000 against 2001–03, a potential indicator of supply that, the authors note, could also mark supply-reduction activity. In VIDUS, a prospective cohort of people who inject drugs in Vancouver interviewed every 6 months, daily heroin use reported from May 1996 to December 2004 was compared between 1996–2000 and 2001–04 by GEE logistic regression, with potential confounders including methadone use and residence in the Downtown Eastside. Editors' note: the death series is titled drug-induced deaths in its source (reference 19, p. 694); no series measures heroin purity, price or availability directly, none covers an area smaller than the Downtown Eastside, and none goes beyond 2003 (December 2004 for the cohort); the paper does not mention supervised injection.

extracted: In VIDUS, 1587 participants provided 13 609 data points at which daily heroin use could be assessed between May 1996 and December 2004. Adjusted for daily cocaine injection, daily crack use, sex-trade involvement, current methadone use, age, Downtown Eastside residence, Aboriginal ethnicity and gender, daily heroin injection was less likely in 2001–04 than in 1996–2000 (adjusted odds ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.50–0.61, P<0.001). Broken down into two-year periods, the proportion reporting daily use was 36.5% in 1997/98, 32.6% in 1999/00, 23.3% in 2001/02 and 20.8% in 2003/04, with no counts or denominators; other drugs did not fall similarly, and methamphetamine use rose significantly (data not shown). Editors' note: self-reported, in one cohort, and not split by area; 2001 is not shown apart from 2002, and nothing is given for 2005. The study cites this paper (its reference 44; Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 1434, 1437) for drug-use patterns that stayed largely constant from 2001 to 2005, with daily heroin injecting of 24% in 2001 and 25% in 2005, daily cocaine injecting of 17% and 15%, and stable methadone and other treatment use (anchor 5). None of these figures is in this paper, whose cohort data end in December 2004, show daily heroin injection lower after 2000 (and 2.5 percentage points lower in 2003/04 than in 2001/02, editors' calculation), and include no yearly figures for daily cocaine injection or methadone use. The authors' reply cites a different 2006 paper by the same five authors (same journal, volume 101, pages 623–625) and a 2009 web report for stable daily heroin use (anchor 12); neither is on file.

extracted: The authors conclude that massive decreases in markers of heroin use were seen in western Canada coinciding with the Australian heroin shortage, despite no increases in funding to Canadian enforcement efforts, and that external global heroin supply forces deserve greater investigation and credence as an explanation of the Australian shortage; they acknowledge that supply may instead have been diverted elsewhere, or production switched to other drugs such as methamphetamine. Limitations they state: overdose statistics and seizure data may be poor proxies for heroin use; the measures were not counted at the same level, and fiscal years put 4 months of post-shortage data in the period before the shortage for naloxone; Canada has no standardized longitudinal measures of street heroin purity, although other studies (cited) found ambulance visits and overdose mortality statistics to correlate strongly with street purity. Funding: the cohort is supported by the US National Institutes of Health and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research; the article has no conflict-of-interest statement. Editors' note: the paper's evidence for unchanged Canadian enforcement is one citation, with no data shown; its statement that reduced heroin availability on Vancouver's streets was widely reported in the media cites a paper on HIV treatment (its reference 17); it measured neither heroin purity nor price.
